Mapping thefts from vehicles in Vancouver: specimen answer

Return to the exercise.

In R, like in many programming languages, there is usually more than one way to complete a task. This code shows one way to complete this exercise. There are other ways to organise this code that are equally good and achieve the same result, but the code below tries to balance making the code efficient with making it easy to read. If your code is different from the code here, read through the notes below the answer and use those to decide whether you prefer your own approach or the specimen answer below. You can also use the notes to improve your own code.

WarningThe specimen answer expects your computer to be set up as outlined in the book.

The online textbook sets out how to install the software you need for crime mapping with R and set up your computer to store files in particular places. The specimen answer below assumes that you have followed those instructions and that your computer is set up as described in the book. If you have not done so, the code in the specimen answer may not run correctly.

Complete script

# This script produces a dot map of thefts from vehicles in Vancouver in 2020

# Load packages
pacman::p_load(here, httr2, sf, sfhotspot, tidyverse)

# Download the original data and keep a local copy
request(
  "https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/vancouver_thefts.csv.gz"
) |>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "vancouver_thefts.csv.gz"))

# Read and wrangle data
thefts_from_vehicles <- here("data", "raw", "vancouver_thefts.csv.gz") |>
  read_csv() |>
  # Convert column names to snake-case
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  # Convert object to an object that understands each row represents a location
  # on the Earth's surface
  st_as_sf(coords = c("x", "y"), crs = "EPSG:32610") |>
  # Keep only the rows in the dataset relating to thefts from vehicles
  filter(type == "Theft from Vehicle")

# Create a dot map of thefts from vehicles
hotspot_map(
  thefts_from_vehicles,
  basemap_type = "cartodark",
  alpha = 0.25,
  colour = "orange3",
  size = 0.5
)

Download the complete R script

Why this code is organised this way

Load packages first. R can only use functions from packages that are loaded. The easiest way to load packages is to load them all at the very start of a script, so that it’s easy to see at a glance all the packages that a particular script needs. That means that, for example, if you are writing a later part of a long R script and you want to use a function from a particular package, it is easy to go to the start of the code and see whether that package is already loaded or whether you need to load it.

Download, then read. The request() and req_perform() functions from the httr2 package save the original CSV file into the data/raw directory so that you have a local copy of the original, unwrangled data. That means that if you later make a mistake in wrangling the data, you can always go back to the original dataset. Note that read_csv() can handle compressed versions of CSV files, including the .csv.gz file downloaded here.

Filter by crime type. The filter() function from the dplyr package filters data based on the values in a specific column, in this case to include only crimes of a specific type. Note that the filter() function performs case-sensitive matching, so it is important to check the spelling, spacing and case of the crime type in the original dataset (in this case, "Theft from Vehicle").

Describe the original coordinates. The original dataset includes locations described using pairs of coordinates specified using UTM zone 10N coordinate reference system, which we can refer to using the code EPSG:32610. To tell R that the numbers in these columns represent locations on the Earth’s surface, we have to specify how these numbers should be translated to locations. To do that we use the st_as_sf() function and the argument crs = "EPSG:32610".

Finish with the map. hotspot_map() converts the SF object we have stored in the thefts_from_vehicles object and plots it on a map with a suitable base map. The basemap helps locate the points, while the supplied colour and size make the points stand out clearly.

Output produced by this code

The code above produces this map. Depending on the design choices you made when writing your code, your map might look slightly different. What matters is that it should be easy for readers to see where the crimes happened and that the base map should support, rather than distracting from, the data layer.

As long as your code correctly and clearly shows the relevant data on a map, it is not necessary for your code to exactly match this specimen answer.
